April 2011 # Resilience - The copper price recovered from below $9,400/t in late February to almost $10,000/t in early March only to slump to a low of $8,990/t on 15th March in the wake of the crisis that hit Japan following the earthquake on 11th March. The price has recovered to trade in a $9,300-9,700/t range, as the impact of the disaster is offset by improving fundamentals elsewhere. - Consumers report some signs of seasonally stronger demand but are more than covered by contracted material. Thus, spot premia are lacklustre. - Exchange inventories in the US and Europe have resumed a gentle downward trend. However, LME inventories in Asia continue to rise as Chinese exports flow out on the back of a sustained negative SHFE-LME arbitrage. |The supply/deman

es.|duction|, Consu|mption|and Stock|s tables.|Forec|ast prod|uction a|llows for|potentia|l| © 2011 CRU International Limited **confidential** Copper Monitor April 2011 www.crumonitor.com # Consumers stay on the sidelines The copper price on the LME recovered in late February and early March to mount another challenge on $10,000/t, with the LME 3-month price hitting a high of $9,980/t on 4th March. This was driven in part by improved investor sentiment about copper due to positive economic news in the USA that saw equities also ris

e. This return of risk appetite came as concerns abated over the negative impact of higher oil prices on economic growth, and therefore copper demand. The price fell below $9,200/t on 10th March, as a result of the revival of the Euro debt crisis and the release of lower than expected February preliminary Chinese copper import data. tsunami on 11th March. However, as the scale of the damage in Japan became clear and the crisis escalated at the Fukushima nuclear reactor, sentiment was further undermined and the LME 3-month price fell to a low of $8,990/t on 15th March. This was followed by some bargain hunting buying, which lifted prices back above $9,000/t. Short covering then helped push prices back over $9,500/t. A test of resistance at $9,200/t on 21st March sparked more buying which in turn spurred a bounce in the 3-month price to a high of $9,755/t on an intra-day trading basis on 24th March. At the time of writing prices were trading around $9,400-9,500/t. As the price has consolidated above $9,000/t, March has also seen the return of a contango between cash and three months prices for the first time since October last year. #### Concentrates to go to other smelters in Japan and China The earthquake and resulting tsunami off the coast of Japan on 11th March forced Mitsubishi Materials Corp to shutdown its Onahama smelter and refinery and Pan Pacific Copper its Hitachi refinery, both of which were located in the affected region. In addition, Dowa has closed its small Kosaka secondary smelter and refinery for safety checks. The three operations accounted for 441kt, or almost 30%, out of total Japanese refined copper production of 1,542kt in 2010. We had expected cathode production in 2011 of 230,000t at Onahama, 210,000t at Hitachi and 12,000t at Kosaka. So a three month shutdown would equate to around 113,000t of cathode. Any spare concentrates arising as a result of the closures will be absorbed either in Japan or China. There is some spare smelting and refining capacity in Japan, as the Japanese smelters have maintained cutbacks due to the tight concentrates market, while capacity expansions in China will mean that smelters there are hungry for raw materials. In addition to the shutdown of refined capacity, the earthquake, tsunami and rolling power cuts are also affecting se

mis producers and therefore refined consumption. Among the brass mills, Furukawa’s Nikko works restarted on 18th March and Mitsui Sumitomo Metal Mining’s plant at Saitama restarted a day later. Kitz Metal Works brass rod plant stopped due to power outage, but has also now restarted. The only two plants not yet back in operation are Mitsui’s and Furukawa’s copper foil plants. Major wirerod mills are located outside the area directly affected by the earthquake and tsunami. Overall, we do not expect that semis production will be affected for very long. The immediate impact of the disaster in Japan will affect semis production to a lesser degree than refined production. This assessment is supported by the fact that CRU understands Japanese producers and © 2011 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 2 of 16 Copper Monitor April 2011 www.crumonitor.com traders have bought some material from Chinese bonded warehouse to cover contractual commitments. Given the disruptions to Japanese production, our estimate of Q1 refined output has fallen marginally. We expect that in the very short term shipments of concentrate on the water will take time to make their way to new destinations. This material will be processed, but at a later date than previously expected, meaning refined production may be pushed back compared to expectations before the earthquake struck. The Japanese situation has, as expected, applied upward pressure to spot treatment terms for concentrates, with reports of trading taking place at terms of around $120/12.0¢ in mid-March. The Indian smelters have been active in sourcing material at these levels, and we have also heard reports that the Chinese are back – as Japanese refined output sees greater direct impact from the earthquake/tsunami than semis Significant Japanese copper facilities Kosaka

Recovery and reconstruction in Japan should begin in H2 and gather pace into 2012, with cathode demand following a similar pattern. The dip in the short term will be made up and we expect cumulative consumption between 2011 and 2013 will be the same as forecast prior to the quake. In part this is based on the experience from other such natural disasters, particularly the Kobe earthquake in Japan in January 1995. #### Spot market subdued... Elsewhere, the spot physical market remained quite subdued over the past month, as consumers in all regions appear to have booked enough material on contract to meet their needs. There are some signs of seasonally stronger

demand beginning to feed through, but these are tentative and confined to industrial end uses.  Construction activity is quiet across all regions, so the largest end use for copper remains a major drag on demand at the moment.  Moreover, an LME price above $9,000/t is keeping restocking activity at bay and the relative abundance of spot metal even allows some destocking (i.e. consumers do not need to hold as much material).  As a result, exchange stocks continued to rise throughout Q1 2011 (up by about 120,000t) ahead of the surplus we now estimate for in the first quarter of this year (14,000t). 

Meanwhile, in Europe semis producers report that they are seeing seasonally stronger growth begin to come through.  However, sustained demand from industrial sectors over the winter months means that the sequential increase in Q2 is likely to be less pronounced than in a typical year, though will still be evident.  Northern Europe remains much more buoyant than the moribund southern European countries, with German demand still streets ahead of other countries.  The lack of spot sales finally saw the premium in Europe succumb and tumble to $35-60/t currently, down from $50-90/t last month.  This is the lowest level since the depths of the financial crisis in Q1 2009.  In the US, premiums have risen by a full cent to 5.0-6.5¢/lb, solely reflecting rising freight costs, even though there are some early signs of an uptick in seasonal demand from industrial end users. 

#### ...including in China 

In China, semis producers report that they have destocked somewhat since the start of the year, while endusers restocked slightly in January ahead of the New Year in February.  Sustained high prices in March mean that there have been few signs of a further significant restock, except by those consumers who

- bought once the SHFE price fell below the key level of RMB70,000/t from 10<sup>th</sup> 17<sup>th</sup> March.  Therefore, on balance overall downstream restocking has been largely non-existent thus far in 2011 in China.  As a result, the premium for imported cathode stood at $40-80/t in the week ending 25<sup>th</sup> March, although this was up from the $0-50/t level reported at the end of February.  CRU forecasts that second quarter Chinese industrial production growth will be 13.7% y-o-y. In addition, Q2 is typically a seasonally stronger quarter for copper consumption in China compared to Q1.  Given the overall low stock levels reported at consumers, we would therefore expect copper demand to pick up in Q2. 

From 17<sup>th</sup> March, SHFE warehouses now include two bonded warehouses.  The stock held in these warehouses has been steady at just over 30,000t.  Tax-paid metal fell to 142,118t on 24<sup>th</sup> March, from 158,254t on the 10<sup>th</sup> March.  We estimate that stock in other bonded warehouses rose by an estimated 40,000t

in March, taking the total estimated bonded material to 570,000t (30,000t SHFE and 540,000t of unreported metal). For the moment the market appears to be looking ahead to the tighter conditions later in the year and are discounting the high stocks in China. We attribute the bulk of the rise of more than 30,000t in LME stocks in Asia over the past month to metal flowing out of China due to SHFE-LME arbitrage trade activity. A significant wild card in China that could precipitate an increase in exports is the build up in stocks of copper that has been imported as collateral for loans. These “collateral stocks” have arisen as banks have tightened credit availability to rein in inflation, and traders report that these account for about 30-40% (some claiming up to 80%) of total bonded warehouse stocks, or 150,000-200,000t. As we have reported in the Copper China Fortnightly, some speculators have used the import of cathode via a letter of credit to then leverage this metal to obtain a further loan using the bonded warehouse receipt as collateral. As these players are using the copper for financing, they overlook the negative arbitrage between SHFE and LME as a cost of doing business. The higher these collateral stocks rise, the greater the potential implosion once credit lines dry up for these speculators. We understand that stocks in bonded warehouses rose to a high of about 600,000t in the first half of the month but have since fallen to around 570,000t at the time of writing. This decline is due to a combination of both buying by Japanese producers and traders to cover their contractual obligations and some sales of “collateral stocks”. Thus, there is a significant stock overhang in China that could become more of a drag on the copper price if consumption does not pick up as forecast in the months ahead and absorb this metal. Prices hold above $9,000/t despite Japanese disasters LME Cash Price Dec 2010–Mar 2011 #### A new floor? The copper price bouncing back above $9,000/t despite a huge natural disaster indicates that the price is building some support at this level. We now expect that LME prices will trade in a volatile range from $9,000/t to $9,700/t over the next month. A break out either side would most likely come from signs that the seasonal upturn is or is not actually coming through, especially in China. On balance we expect that any break out will be to the upside, as the momentum from the broader economic recovery is more likely to lead to consumption growth rising as expected. This would then initiate drawdown in stocks that have built up over the last few months. Price ($/t)

arthquake in Japan caused some disruptions in fabricators’ operations.  However, CRU believes that world copper demand will not be significantly affected since Japan accounts for only 6% of total refined consumption.  Despite the short term negative impact, we believe that reconstruction work will boost copper consumption in the medium term.  In addition, the ongoing social unrest and military action in the Middle East-North Africa region continue to impose increasing downside risks to the global market.  Most importantly, high oil prices impact the outlook for industrial growth.  Furthermore, due to high and volatile copper prices, leading fabricators in the industrialised world expressed their concerns regarding the cash tied up.  As a move to reduce exposure to rising copper prices, **Luvata’s** North American rolled copper products business is asking some clients to buy their own cathode as an alternative to 30-day payment terms. 

## **Copper plate, sheet, strip and foil (PSSF)** 

World copper PSSF production was marginally lower in Q1 2011 compared to the same period a year ago.  We estimate that world output amounted to 490,000t, a 0.7% y-o-y decline.  The figure was also down by 3.3% sequentially.  However, from a regional standpoint, production development in Q1 2011 was a mixed picture.  Supported by a recovery in electrical engineering, US production of copper PSSF advanced by 6.0% y-o-y to 27,000t.  In Europe, Germany continued to lead the way, with output having risen by 10.2% y-o-y to 50,000 in Q1.  This is mainly attributed to strong overseas demand for final products and a strong domestic market. 

Production in North East Asia exhibited a marked slowdown, which was to a large extent an expected one.  In the beginning of 2010, demand from end-use sectors was particularly strong, partially driven by subsidy programmes.  Therefore, the region had largely benefited from the market upturn at the time but we anticipated that the strong growth could not be sustained.  Moreover, the earthquake in Japan affected output only in the second half of March, and therefore the impact on the whole first quarter is limited. We believe that Japanese output declined by 13.4% y-o-y to 60,000t in Q1 2011.  The **Japan Copper and Brass Association** reported that total semis output in February 2011 was up by 1% y-o-y and expected that the figure in March is likely to fall due to the earthquake.  Indeed, major electrodeposited copper foil and rolled copper foil makers such as **JX Nippon Mining & Metals** and **Hitachi Cable** have plants in areas impacted by the earthquake.  It was reported that Taiwanese end-use sectors that consume copper PSSF have been impacted as well.  Examples include display panels, semiconductors, machinery equipment and solar cells. 

Chinese output of copper PSSF amounted to an estimated 162,000t in Q1 2011.  The **China Nonferrous Metals Association** reported that semis output dropped by 2.1% y-o-y in the first two months

of 2011. The decline was attributed to delayed downstream orders due to high copper prices.  We have heard that fabricators maintain low copper stocks and take a cautious approach when making purchases, with volumes only high enough to meet existing orders.  China remains the largest importer of copper PSSF products.  In full year 2010, domestic production totalled 706,000t whilst consumption soared to 937,000t.  There has been a long-term gradual decline in imports, supported by aggressive domestic capacity expansion.  However, due to booming demand, imports have surged once again in early 2011. CRU predicts that imports will fall in the current year as domestic production will be increasingly meeting local consumption needs.  In addition, the market is not expected to grow at last year’s rate.

## **Copper alloy plate, sheet, strip and foil (PSSF)** 

The copper alloy PSSF business is strongly correlated with the copper PSSF product sector due to common end-uses, especially the interconnect segment.  Developments in the electrical & electronic and consumer & general product markets dictate demand for both copper and copper alloy PSSF.  Hence, the analysis provided in the copper PSSF segment is relevant to this product sector as well. 

World production of copper alloy PSSF fell by 1.8% y-o-y to 507,000t in Q1 2011.  This product segment exhibited robust output growth in 2010, expanding by 26.7% and surpassed earlier expectations.  One of the reasons that copper alloy PSSF performed so well in 2010 was that it was only marginally exposed to the troubled construction sector.  Hence, it fully benefited from the recovery in electrical & electronic and consumer & general product markets last year.  However, production growth in Q1 2011 was uneven across regions.  Regions that boomed last year saw a slowdown in the beginning of 2011, while those still suffering from the impact of the global financial crisis in the beginning of last year experienced growth or contracted only modestly in Q1 2011. 

Production of copper alloy PSSF in the US declined by 3.3% y-o-y to 65,000t in Q1 2011.  Despite the decline, we believe that this production level represents a positive sign as it is compared against a strong quarter in 2010.  German production of copper alloy PSSF amounted to 54,000t, a 3.8% increase from the same period a year ago.  Output exhibited a very strong turnaround last year and there are still signs of further growth due to robust demand from bespoke domestic engineering sectors.  Q1 2011 output represented an 80% increase from the same period in 2009.  This growth was largely generated by enduse demand from emerging markets.  Moreover, Italian copper alloy PSSF production rose by 16% y-o-y to 12,000t in Q1 2011. 

North East Asian copper alloy PSSF production decreased by 13.7% y-o-y to 83,000t in Q1 2011.  The contraction was stee

per than in copper PSSF, however that followed an aggressive recovery in 2010. Japanese production reached 38,000t in Q1 2011, down from 46,000t in the same period a year ago. We understand that despite the current slowdown and the impact due to the earthquake, Japan will continue to be an important producer in this segment. This is supported by technical know-how and patents. We estimate that Chinese production of copper alloy PSSF totalled 162,000t in Q1 2011, down by 2.1% from the same period a year ago. Output in 2010 was 790,000t, up by 21.5% from 2009. Similar to copper PSSF, China is not yet self-sufficient in copper alloy PSSF products. ## **Contemporary trends in copper and alloy flat rolled products** One of the reasons this product category performed so strongly in 2010 was that it was used by high-end final products, the markets which are on a long-term rising trend. For instance, smartphones, flat screens, computers and hybrid vehicles are high value added products that benefit from the superior properties of copper. CRU believes that this product group is one of the most immune when we consider copper substitution or rationing issues. High performance and compact size are crucial characteristics that the above final products need to feature. In addition, despite high copper prices, the final price of those products is at a level that covers the cost of using copper. Despite current market challenges, we project that growth prospects for these high-end applications are very promising, and therefore the potential for copper and alloy flat rolled products remains high. A major development is that new flat rolled product capacity is concentrated in Asia. Projects currently in progress are primarily Japanese or Chinese. Examples include automotive connectors and copper foil used in lithium ion batteries. An important research trend is the development of ultra-thin copper foil that can be used in high-end applications such as high-density printing circuit boards. However, in spite of the optimistic market prospects, product miniaturisation is leading to less use of copper per final item sold. © 2011 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 10 of 16 Copper Monitor April 2011 www.crumonitor.com |Copper pla

- Major Japanese copper semis and wire and cable manufacturers were affected by the devastating earthquake. The company’s production equipment at its telecom cable factory experienced damages. **Mitsubishi Shindoh** , a copper and alloy semis fabricator, saw its plumbing operations partially destroyed. **San-Etsu** , a brass bar specialist, shut down production at its Shin-Nitto plant in Ibaraki, without any significant damages reported whatsoever. - The copper industry faces ongoing disruptions due to the devastating earthquake in Japan. **Mitsui Mining & Smelting** reported that there were still plant suspensions at several sites in Saitama, Fukushima and Aomori Prefectures. In addition, **Sumitomo Electric Industries (SEI)** said that **Daikoku Electric Wire’s** sites in Tochigi and Iwate Prefectures continued to be impacted.  Daikoku Electric is a subsidiary of SEI and engages in the production of magnet wire. 

- According to Antaike, **Guangxi Nonferrous Secondary Metals’** 200,000t/y copper wirerod project was approved by **Guangxi Development and Reform Commission** .  Guangxi Nonferrous is mainly engaged in recycling and processing of copper and copper related products. 

- **Ganzhou Jiangwu - La Farga High Speed Railway Copper Materials** will begin its activity in August 2011. The company is a joint venture, with Spain’s **La Farga Group** holding a majority stake. 

- Chilean copper producer **Codelco** expects that new uses of copper, mainly related to its antimicrobial capacity, will boost world copper demand by 300,000t/y within the next eight years. Codelco participates in development programmes which aim to promote the benefits of using copper.

er **Leoni** reported sales of €2.96B in FY2010, up from €2.16B in the previous year. - **Lundin Mining** and **Inmet Mining** announced the termination of the agreement signed on 12<sup>th</sup> January 2011.  The parties have agreed that Inmet's right to a break fee of $120M, in relation to the earlier agreement, will support the unsolicited offer of **Equinox Minerals** to acquire Lundin Mining. 

- **Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold** announced on 29<sup>th</sup> March that copper output from the **Grasberg** copper-gold mine is expected to decline in 2011 by 17% y-o-y. ## **Exploration and Development** 













- On 29<sup>th</sup> March, **Southern Copper Corporation** (SCC) announced the delay of the development of their **Tia Maria** project in Peru. The main reason given is social conflicts with the local community. Tia Maria would be an investment of $1B to produce 120,000t/y of EW cathode at full capacity and was due to start-up in 2012. 

- On 30<sup>th</sup> March, **BHP Billiton** announced that the **Olympic Dam Project** had progressed into the feasibility study phase. However, some formal authorisations are still pending. The project plan is to develop a new open pit copper mine with associated gold and uranium by-products alongside its existing underground operation. Production capacity would increase from around 180,000t/y of copper-in-concentrate to 750,000t/y over the next 30 years. 

- **BHP Billiton** announced the approval of the **Escondida Ore Access** project (EOA), with an investment of $554M. The miner will re

locate the crushing and conveying facilities, currently located inside the main pit. This will enable access to higher grade ore and increase production from 2013 as project is scheduled to be completed by mid calendar year 2012. In 2010, Escondida produced 787,000t of copper-in-concentrate and 300,000t of EW cathode. 

- In early March, **Xstrata Copper** announced that Peruvian authorities have granted the approval of the Environmental and Social Impact Assessment (ESIA) for the US$4.2B **Las Bambas** copper project in southern Peru.  Construction is scheduled to begin in Q3 2011.  Ore processing will begin in Q2 2014, with full production expected by the end of that year.  The mine will initially produce 400,000 t/y of copper-in-concentrates, with significant gold and silver, and also some molybdenum. 

- **Aditya Birla Minerals** has received approval for stage 1 of the re-start of operations at its **Mount Gordon** mine in Queensland and hopes to receive approval for stage 2 by mid-April.  The mine was closed in January 2009.  It had a capacity to produce around 25,000t/y of copper-in-concentrates. 

- In early March, the board of Australia’s **Sandfire Resources** approved the development of its 70,000t/y **DeGrussa** copper-gold project in Western Australia, following the completion of a positive pre-feasibility study.  Open pit and underground mine construction are due to begin in Q2 2011, subject to the finalisation of a project funding package.  Mine production is scheduled to begin in Q1 2012 and the commissioning of the concentrator in Q3.  Production will be 70,000t/y of copper-inconcentrate, with sufficient reserves for a 7-year mine life. 

## **Smelting and Refining** 





- Spot copper concentrate TC/RCs have risen rapidly after the earthquake and tsunami in Japan. **Mitsubishi’s Onahama** smelter and refinery has been closed since the disaster and the company declared force majeure on copper concentrate supply contracts on 21<sup>st</sup> March.  This smelter is located close to the Fukushima nuclear plant with excessive levels of radiation, which makes it unlikely that workers would return to resume operations anytime soon. Spot treatment charges had already begun to rise after the smelter shutdown on expectations that concentrates due to be delivered would have to be re-routed and likely resold. 

- **Pan Pacific Copper (PPC)** has announced that it will be maintaining a production cut at its smelting and refining operations in Southwest Japan during the coming financial year, and may increase the cutback to 15% of capacity.  The company cites scarce raw material supply as the main reason for the cutback, which will result in a reduction in output of 30,000t of refined copper compared with the

- A judge of the Court of Valparaiso ordered the temporary closure of **Codelco’s Ventanas** smelter and refinery. - **Yunnan Copper** completed the maintenance work at its **Kunming** smelter more than a month ahead of schedule. - **Sterlite** has been awarded a further extension to the stay against the High Court order to close the **Tuticorin** smelter, allowing it to continue operating. - China’s Ministry of Environmental Protection has ordered **Xinjiang Wuxin Copper** to stop the construction of its 100kt/y copper smelting and refining project for environmental reasons.
